newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: East European summit winds up, EU gulf widens.
newsitem.headline: East European summit winds up, EU gulf widens.

text.p: Central and Eastern European states ended three days of talks on Friday that failed to conceal a widening gulf between nations on a fast track to integration with the West and those being left behind.

Heads of state and government, ministers, central bankers and top company officials from the region met for the second Central and Eastern European Economic Summit in the city of Salzburg to discuss priorities for the region.

But the debate was overshadowed by NATO's decision earlier in the week to limit its expansion to the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary and news on Thursday that the European Commission would recommend starting EU entry talks with only the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia and Cyprus.

Analysts and politicians agreed the cachet of membership in exclusive Western clubs like the EU and NATO would carry great economic weight, boosting foreign investment and raising confidence. But they shied away from quantifying the benefits.

"The invitation (to join NATO) probably does ratchet up our standing among foreign investors," said Karel Kovanda, the Czech deputy foreign minister. "(But) we do not know how to quantify what it is going to cost us, never mind quantify the benefits."
Countries that seemed to have missed out on the first round of the EU's eastward expansion made little effort to conceal their bitter disappointment in Salzburg.

Slovak President Michal Kovac urged the West not to abandon the fledgling democracies of formerly communist Europe. "I hope that the member countries of the European Union...will not turn their backs on Slovakia," he told Reuters in an interview.

His Romanian counterpart Emil Constantinescu described the comments by Brussels officials as overly hasty. "I believe this...does not reflect the point of view of the heads of state and governments of member countries," he said.
Analysts have warned that a decision to limit the number of EU entrants, coming so soon after NATO's move, may create a new order of winners and losers in a politically vulnerable region.

"There is a danger that the EMU (European economic and monetary union) bloc will suddenly become a large and closed economic region. This could in turn lead to a trade fortress in Europe," said one economist.

While politicians rejoiced or lamented the EU stance, Central and East European central bankers concentrated their minds on the economic impacts of the bloc's expansion and the likely effects of Europe's planned single currency, due for launch on January 1, 1999.
For the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Estonia and Slovenia the euro's successful introduction is the final hurdle between them and the start of EU entry negotiations.
"Central European countries are interested in a timely introduction of the euro as a prerequisite for starting enlargement talks," said Gyorgy Suranyi, president of the National Bank of Hungary.

Former communist states that appeared to have missed out on the first wave of the bloc's eastward expansion fixed their sights on a more distant goal -- the timing of their integration into the EU and survival outside.

"Latvia is strongly committed to becoming a full member of the European Union," said Latvian central bank head Einars Repse. He played down doomsday scenarios of a strong euro area drawing investment away from the transition economies while stemming trade flows between Eastern and Western Europe.
Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovenia and Estonia, busy preparing for tougher competition inside the European Union, saw their economies well on the road to integration.
"I believe the Czech economy will become more and more financially integrated in the EU, regardless of whether it is a member or not," said Czech central banker Josef Tosovsky.
